analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' windfall profits above $75 a barrel and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill would tax 100% of oil company revenue above $75 a barrel and rebate it to individual taxpayers, but it drew zero cosponsors and has sat untouched in the Ways and Means Committee since its introduction on May 13, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill puts a 100% excise tax on every barrel of crude oil sold above $75, applying only to companies that extract or import more than 100,000 barrels a day. All the money collected would go into a fund and be paid back to individual taxpayers as refundable rebates. The tax would stay in effect until the President declares hostilities with Iran over, the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, and oil falls below $75 a barrel.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers, who would receive rebates funded entirely by a tax on large oil companies' profits during the war-driven price spike. The rebate is refundable, so even people who owe little or no income tax would get it, and the Treasury would have to run an outreach program to make sure people claim it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Individual taxpayers during the oil price spike

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 100% excise tax on the portion of each barrel's price above $75 (West Texas Intermediate), applying to US-extracted and imported crude, gasoline, and diesel from companies handling more than 100,000 barrels a day.

Sends every dollar collected into an 'Iran War Gasoline Price Relief Fund' and pays it out to eligible individuals as a refundable credit against income tax, meaning low-income filers who owe little tax still receive the money.

The tax remains in force until the President declares hostilities with Iran have ceased, the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened, and oil falls below $75 a barrel, so relief is tied to the actual crisis ending rather than a fixed calendar date.
Requires the Treasury to run a 'robust and comprehensive' outreach program within 30 days of enactment so taxpayers know they are eligible and get help claiming the credit.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies — those extracting or importing more than 100,000 barrels per day — which would surrender all revenue above $75 per barrel on US-extracted oil and on oil, gasoline, and diesel brought into the country. Smaller producers under that threshold are exempt.

drawbacks.text: Because the tax is levied on each barrel, oil companies could pass some or all of it through to consumers at the pump, raising gasoline prices during a crisis; the rebate is a flat per-person amount, so households that drive more — rural workers, long commuters — could end up net losers.
The $75 threshold rises with inflation after 2026, and the tax automatically ends once oil falls below the (inflating) threshold, so the relief shrinks over a long crisis.
The 100,000 barrels-per-day threshold exempts smaller producers, giving them a competitive advantage over major companies and leaving part of the windfall untaxed.

Rebates go to eligible individuals filing for the credit while excluding dependents and nonresident aliens, and the flow of money depends entirely on continued oil revenues at high prices, making the payment size unpredictable quarter to quarter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: during a war-driven oil spike, it claws back windfall revenue from the largest oil companies and hands it to households. The design has honest weaknesses — the tax could partly reach the pump before rebates arrive, the flat rebate does not track how much fuel a household actually buys, and the exemption for producers under 100,000 barrels a day lets part of the windfall escape. Whether it nets out for a given family depends on how much they drive and how much of the tax companies absorb versus pass on.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 13, 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on May 13, 2026, proposing a 100% windfall excise tax on oil priced above $75 a barrel, with all proceeds rebated to individual taxpayers until the Iran hostilities end and oil falls back below $75.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation, and no further action of any kind has been taken since.
No other member of the House — Democrat or Republican — signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the largest oil companies are better off: the war-era profits above $75 a barrel remain untaxed, and no hearing or vote has been scheduled on a bill with zero cosponsors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil companies keep untaxed windfall profits

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 13, 2026, proposing a 100% tax on oil profits above $75 a barrel with the proceeds rebated to taxpayers.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 13, 2026 and has taken no action since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and sat in a Republican-led committee.

industries.note: Companies extracting or importing more than 100,000 barrels a day would surrender every dollar of price above $75 per barrel on US crude, crude condensates, gasoline, and diesel. Their war-driven windfall comes directly out of consumers' fuel bills, so in this bill their interest runs against the public's.
Producers under the 100,000 barrels-per-day threshold are exempt, so they could sell at the same elevated wartime prices without paying the tax, gaining a cost advantage over the majors.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action since the May 2026 referral, and a Republican-led Ways and Means Committee controlling the calendar, the bill will almost certainly die in committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Most bills referred to committee never get a hearing, and this one has no visible support beyond its sponsor.
